newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian President Tudjman home after treatment.
newsitem.headline: Croatian President Tudjman home after treatment.

text.p: Croatia's ailing President Franjo Tudjman returned on Saturday from medical treatment in Washington to reassert his authority after the first popular protests in years shook the capital.
Looking visibly pale and thinner, with hollow cheeks, Tudjman stepped off the plane at Zagreb airport to be met by senior officials, including defence and interior ministers.
About half a dozen citizens gathered in front of the airport to greet him. "We don't want democracy, we want Croatia," one of their banners said.
"I feel well, but after 11 days of treatment and 12 hours in a car and a plane, even younger people would be tired," Tudjman said in a frail voice at a brief press conference at the airport.
U.S. sources have said the 74-year-old president was being treated for stomach cancer while state media in Croatia described his ailment as "digestive problems".

Shortly after the arrival Tudjman met U.S. General Jacques Klein, head of the last Serb-held enclave in Croatia, administered by the United Nations. Eastern Slavonia is due to gradually return under Zagreb rule next year.

"He's on top of the issues, he's very good. Sometimes he is much more dynamic...than the government. He wants peaceful reintegration and is willing to cut through a lot of bureaucracy to get it done," Klein told reporters after the meeting.

He said the reintegration, monitored by some 5,000 peacekeepers was "on the right track" and voting for a local administration could be held next year, within the countrywide local and regional elections.
In open defiance of Tudjman's ruling HDZ party some 100,000 people rallied in downtown Zagreb on Wednesday and Thursday to support a popular independent radio the government tried to shut down.
The protest, which grew into a demand for more democracy in the former Yugoslav republic, was the first since Croatia gained independence in 1991.

Last week the opposition walked out of parliament in protest at the autocratic HDZ's refusal to discuss power-sharing in Zagreb, where Tudjman has refused to accept the defeat of the HDZ by an opposition coalition in local polls last year.
Raising his voice and banging the fist against the table, Tudjman implied he would not cede power in the capital.

"The Zagreb crisis will be solved only when prudent members of the opposition realise that the crisis was not a coincidence but an attempt to destabilise the Croatian authorities which secured Croatia's sovereignty," he said.

Tudjman has often been criticised for his authoritarian rule. The Council of Europe in May shelved Croatia's bid for admission to punish it for its mistreatment of the independent media and ethnic minorities, and for the situation in Zagreb.
Croatia was formally admitted to the Council in November after pledging to comply with its requirements.
The attempt to close Radio 101 prompted criticism of the nationalist government in Europe and the United States but Tudjman appeared to brush off the reprimands.

"Croatian democracy will secure human rights for minorities, as well as freedom of the media. We will not allow solutions to be imposed (on us) from the outside...from countries unable to solve their own problems," he said.
